title: The Three Doors of Liberation
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: The talk's main teaching is that true liberation comes from understanding the interconnectedness of all things and letting go of our fixed notions about ourselves and the world. By recognizing that everything is empty of a separate self, we can transform and grow in the present moment, rather than getting stuck in past regrets or future desires. This involves stopping our striving for goals and desires, and instead cultivating mindfulness and presence to experience life more fully and authentically.

sentences.text: Good evening again, everyone.
Thanks to everyone who came tonight, and also thank you for returning people for the second part of this talk.
I appreciate it.
Tonight I'm going to continue with some more foundational teachings of the Buddha.
As I said last week when we were talking about the three dharma seals of impermanence, no-self, and nirvana, suffering, I feel like these are tied to those, that they're a set.
So tonight I called the talk Stepping Through the Three Doors of Liberation, and I want to continue with that.
If you didn't have a chance to hear the first talk and all of our talks, you can find them on YouTube easily.
Last week I mentioned that these teachings are really a chance, an invitation to explore for yourself, as the Buddha encouraged.

I had said that they're not things to believe in, but rather tools to look deeply into the workings of our own minds, and a way to touch what is beyond our perceived notions about the way things work as human beings.
The first talk was Uncovering the Three Dharma Seals, and tonight we're going to be stepping into the Three Doors of Liberation.
These teachings are always available.
We only have to have a willingness to explore them, to uncover their true meaning.

Last week I talked a little bit about the two truths before I got into the three dharma seals, and I just want to mention those again, because it's really helpful to realize that sometimes teachings are offered through the realm of the conditioned, our world that we're used to living in, the historic world.
And sometimes teachings are pointing to a deeper reality, the ultimate reality, the unconditioned, the absolute realm.
Mari had mentioned maybe I shouldn't give so many descriptions for these things because it's confusing, when I call it the unconditioned world, ultimate dimension.
So anyway, I'll try not to use too many words to describe them.
But really, we live in this world of the conditioned, and always we're also part of this deeper, unconditioned realm.

When the Buddha gave the five remembrances that we talked about last week (we are of a nature to grow old and have ill health, to be separated from the ones we love, and at some point die), he was speaking about the nature of things in this world, in this historic realm, this conditioned realm.
And Thich Nhat Hanh says that the Buddha wanted us to get used to the reality of this, to make friends with our fears around these truths about living in our world.
When Avalokiteshvara was speaking in the Heart Sutra about the realm of no birth and no death, she was referring then to a deeper reality, the absolute, the unconditioned realm.
I won't say any more words.
They're both true, and in fact never apart.
We are always in touch with both of these realities, and we don't usually realize it because we're living through our perceptions and notions about how things are.
Our mission, if we decide to accept it, is to more easily touch the ultimate, unconditioned realm right now, in this moment.
It is the realm of no coming and no going, no after, and no before.
It is a realm free from our thoughts, ideas, and notions.
The three doors of liberation include emptiness, which is shunyata in Pali, signlessness, which is animita, and aimlessness, which is apranihita.
The first door I want to talk about this evening is emptiness.
By the way, last week we stopped for some comments, and I forgot to send the mic around, so in the recording there was just silence.
Tonight I'll ask somebody to help me with the microphone.
So the first door is emptiness.
The first time we hear this word, I think many of us are confused, maybe have a negative reaction to it.
Emptiness sounds a lot like nothingness.
Similarly, last week I spoke of no self, and that also may bring up some idea of nothingness.
In fact, to me, both no self and emptiness are truly words to express how things are in the ultimate realm.
As Thich Nhat Hanh explained, to be empty means to be empty of something.
For example, when you say a cup is empty, it may be empty of water or tea, but it's full of all of these other molecules of air.
So when you hear that something's empty, you want to ask: empty of what?
And the answer is empty of a separate self.
This means also that it's full of everything else.
So we're full of everything and empty of a separate independent self.
Last week I spoke about how I discovered that these blood cells that were in me were me.
If we start taking things apart, it would be never ending.
Things that are on the inside: red blood cells and then the iron in them, the bacteria, the organs.
What about things on the outside?
The food, the tea, the water, the air.
When does food stop being food and start being me?
If it were possible to remove all of these components in me, there would be nothing left of me.
Being empty of a separate self truly allows for the possibility of change, but if we really look deeply, we see that we are made up of all of these non-self elements.
Not having a separate self, being totally interconnected with everything, allows for movement and flow.
We're not stagnant entities.
Change and transformation are possible in this lifetime because we're not fixed objects.
So emptiness in Buddhist teachings means empty of a separate self.
It doesn't mean nothing.
Everything without exception is like this.
Everything is interconnected and interdependent.
If we think we can survive on our own, we're not understanding what we really are.
We truly understand we are supported by all things and all things are in here.
And the reverse is true.
We support all things.
So, are there any comments about emptiness?
In the Diamond Sutra, we were taught that a human being is not independent of other sentient and non-sentient beings.
In order to take care of ourselves, we have to also take care of all of these non-human species.
And I think we're really struggling with that right now, our world in general, with so much out of balance.
But it's important to keep that in mind, and I'll talk about it a little bit more in a second.
The second door of liberation is the door of signlessness.
This refers to the recognition that we, as human beings, like to conceptualize and label everything.
When we see something, our brain labels it: there's a sign for it, an image is formed.
Often if it's something we haven't encountered before, it might be fresh.
But if it's something that we've already encountered, if we already have a pathway set up for that, a lot of times we don't even really look at it.
Our brain skips over it and sometimes thinks, "Oh, I know what I'm doing."
And we just don't even go there.
We categorize it and make assumptions about it and we develop notions about it.
We give it a common name.
Then we give it a full, maybe scientific name, and think that somehow is more correct in how we're describing it.
For instance, I may see a yellow and black and green thing in the garden, and I recognize it.
"Oh, it's a sunflower."
I know its name, sunflower.
And then more precisely, I may even know that it's a Helianthus annus belonging to the daisy family Asteraceae.
We do that with so many different things that we see.
I'm not saying that we don't need these signs to live, to function in our world, in our society, on roads, in the traffic.
Our world is so full of signs that we don't recognize sometimes the forms before we've already attached a name or a sign to it.
We don't see the flower, the sunflower.
We don't see it as a sunflower, or not even a sunflower, just as it is.
We really determine the value of something by how we as humans and cultures define it.
What about something that's labeled as a weed?
Is there some ultimate truth in that, in our head, that we think that it's a weed?
It instantly brings this judgment of good or bad or worthy or not worthy to exist.
Truly, it's a created term for a living plant that originally had no label.
Things in our world are determined to be useful or not useful, good or not good, desired or not desired, et cetera.
So it's valuable to recognize these signs and recognize what's obscured by them.
It's often helpful to develop awareness around how much of our society and world are quickly judged by our brain and categorized.
We live with a lot of notions about everything.
Thich Nhat Hanh says that until we break through these signs, we can't really touch this ultimate reality.
We can't really touch what's beneath them because our head is full of them.
So it's a great relief, really, to break through some of the signs and to touch the world of signlessness, which is also called nirvana, a world free of notions and ideas.
I'm sure some of you are familiar with the Diamond Sutra.
It's a very famous early sutra.
The full name of the Diamond Sutra is the Diamond that Cuts through Illusion.
And it encourages us to see the four notions that we've created.
These four notions are notions of a self, a separate self, notions of a human being, notions of a living being, and notions of a life span.
We've already talked about the sign of self.
We think there are things that are self and things that are not self.
As we've explored, in reality, in a deeper way, there are really no true boundaries.
We see that we really don't have an independent separate self.
But we also get caught in the sign of a person or a human being.
We separate humans from other forms, both animate and inanimate.
What this separation causes and justifies so often is a path of exploitation.
We are justified in things for our benefit because they are not human.
As we talked about earlier, when we look deeply, we can see that everything we do, whether it's to other species or to the earth, directly affects all of us, whether we see it or not.
Our use of plastics and pesticides, for instance, are in all of us and in other species all over the earth now.
There is no way to keep separate from them.
Even the sign of a living being is not really separate from an insentient being.
We know that many things in our body are insentient.
The many minerals that make up my blood and my tissues are totally interconnected and integrated in my cells and my bones and blood.
If they weren't there, I wouldn't be here either.
Lastly, we think of a life span.
We think that we have a period of time between being born and dying.
We are alive as a separate self for a specific time with a beginning and an end.
But when we see that everything in our body is in the process of being born and living and dying, nothing is truly lost.
Everything is still here in the present moment.
So we can let go of some of the fear of our ending.
The other day, I heard a podcast that someone else was listening to.
They were talking about all of these things that we need to do with our science and technology.
One of those things, the person that was talking said that he heard that the most important thing we can do is to figure out how to deal with old age, because old age is a disease.
A number one priority for science and technology should be to eliminate old age and allow us to live productive lives for much longer.
These statements fit into actually the four notions that we so often take as reality from the Diamond Sutra.
For me, these statements reflect the identifying first as a human being, and second as having a life span.
For me, those statements are very human and self-centric.
They come from a world based on everything revolving around me and human beings.
I always remember Thich Nhat Hanh's answer to a child's question.
The child asked, "Do you remember any of your past lives?"
And he said, "Yes.
When I practice looking deeply, I see that at some time in my past, I was a rock, a tree, a squirrel, a bird, a fish, a cloud, a river.
If I continue to look deeply, I see that I am still a rock, a cloud, a mountain, a river, and a squirrel.
I continue to be them."
I have been all of these things, and so have you.
And we continue to be all of them.
They are still in us.
We still inter-are with them.
Lastly, I wanted to look at aimlessness.
Here's another word that may cause some confusion or resistance.
The dictionary's definition of aimless is lacking a clear purpose or goal or direction.
I think in our society, we've added on a sign to this, if you will, a negative connotation of being lazy, without a goal or achieving or making something of your life.
In the Buddhist context, aimlessness is really referring to letting go of achieving, letting go of pushing towards getting something in the future, letting go of constant striving for one more thing.
It's an understanding that we already have and are really everything we need.
So Master Dogen encourages practice realization, meaning that our reason for practicing is a means of uncovering what is already here.

Instead of going from point A to point B to get something, we already are Buddha nature and we don't realize it because all of these notions and concepts that we've been talking about are in the forefront.
There's a lot of Buddhist literature about letting go of the desire to obtain something, letting go of a notion that tells us, "If only I could get that college degree, then I'll rest easy.
If only I have this X amount of money, then I will be happy."
Of course, the desire for things is endless.
Even the desire for small things.
"I've got to get that new toy."
Of course we've all been there.

I can't remember where I heard this, but I was watching, I think it was at Dharma Talk, I was watching how this person was recalling how desperately he wanted this new train that he saw in the window of a store.
If only he could get that new train, he would be happy for the rest of his life.
He promised his mom that if he only got that, he would never ask for anything else ever again.
And he got it.
So you know how the rest of the story goes.
At first he played with it all day long, and the second day he played with it all day long, and then little by little he didn't play with it quite as much, and in a little while it was forgotten.
This happens over and over.
And we tell ourselves sometimes, "But this time is different.
This time it's really what I want."
So it's good to pay attention to our desire and to our cravings.
When we've gone down that path so many times, it's just a little easier to recognize it and to know what the outcome is if we keep being on that path.
We can more quickly see how all of these things are impermanent, but it's not easy to understand that all things are like that.
So aimlessness is about the ability to stop.
Shamantha in Pali.
Thich Nhat Hanh says that Buddhist meditation has two aspects, samanta and vipassana, looking deeply.
They bring us insight and liberate us from suffering and afflictions.
But he says the practice of stopping is fundamental, because if we can't stop, we can't have insight.
It's really an art, I think, to be able to stop.
Stopping our thinking, our habit energies, our forgetfulness, strong emotions that rule us.
It doesn't mean that we're trying to get rid of things, because I think in years past I really felt like what I was wanting to do is get rid of the things that I didn't like about myself.
And it really is not that.
It's just giving ourselves a chance to really just be in the present and take a little bit of time to really...
Sometimes that's so important instead of blundering ahead and taking action too quickly.
So it's really just about giving ourselves space to breathe.
That's what allows us to maybe be able to come back, to have the mindfulness, to have the vipassana.
There is no place for transformation but here in the present moment.
Everything is here and now.
If we ignore this moment in pursuit of future or regrets about the past, we're giving up our possibility of transformation.
This is why we sit.
We have a stronger possibility of being present, being in the here and now.
Over time this becomes a path that we can settle into a little easier.
And if we carry this presence into our walking and into our drinking tea and cleaning the kitchen, they become more alive with our presence.
So that is the three doors of liberation in a nutshell.
We have plenty of time this week.
Last week, I'm sorry, I just kept going on and on and we had no time and I looked at my watch and it was already 8:30.
Tonight we have a little bit of time, so maybe we can get into some triads.
If you saw the talk last week and things that we talked about this week, just pick out something that resonates with you.
Just pick something out that you're working on in your practice right now and talk about that with your partners.
Then if we have time we can take a few comments from the group.
So it's about five after, so I think...
